previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with Type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis s/p gastric pacer presented with acute nausea and vomiting, one week after a prior hospitalization for similar symptoms. She had recently received a Botox injection for gastroparesis and reported coffee-ground emesis. She was admitted for inability to tolerate oral intake and managed with IV fluids, antiemetics (ondansetron, metoclopramide, compazine), and proton pump inhibition. Her hypertension, exacerbated by vomiting and anxiety, was controlled with IV metoprolol and transitioned to oral lisinopril. Abdominal imaging showed no obstruction or ileus. She gradually improved, tolerating a soft diet and oral medications. Her sodium was noted to be low (130) on discharge but asymptomatic; outpatient labs were ordered. She was discharged home in stable condition with new prescriptions for metoclopramide, pantoprazole, ondansetron, and lisinopril, and follow-up planned with gastroenterology for pacer evaluation.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled

Brief Hospital Course:
# Nausea and vomiting - The patient's symptoms were identical to 
recent admissions, all thought to be related to her intractable 
diabetic gastroparesis. She had been taking her reglan, zofran, 
PPI as prescribed to good effect until the morning of admission. 
Blood sugars had been within her recent range of 200-300.  Upon 
presentation, she did have urine ketones although blood ketones 
were not checked. Her gap was 15. Investigation for infectious 
causes as well as myocardial ischemia were unrevealing. Early 
DKA is possible although starvation ketosis is equally possible. 
Upon presentation, she was made NPO with IV fluids along with 
standing reglan and PPI, prn zofran, prn compizine and ativan, 
all IV.  The patient's vomiting improved over the 36 hours prior 
to discharge, after she had been restricted to 5 ml sips of 
clears followed by toast and tea.  At discharge the patient was 
tolerating po medications and her tea and toast diet, with 
improved nausea.  She will continue a low-fat, low-fiber BRAT 
diet with education and careful advancement.  She is scheduled 
to see Dr. ___ in his ___ clinic for follow up 
including possible enteric pacemaker interrogation on the 
afternoon of discharge.  She is also planning on scheduling an 
appointment with ___ for social therapy.
.  
# Hypertension - The patient's blood pressures were controlled 
with IV metoprolol followed by lisinopril 10 mg PO (her regimen 
restarted at the end of her last hospitalization) by discharge, 
to good effect. 
. 
# DM1 - Blood sugars had been elevated.  A1c was 8.3 in ___.  
She was followed by ___ consultant.  She is on her prior 
long-acting insulin regimen plus an attenuated short-acting 
regime pending advancement of her diet beyond her current BRAT 
diet.  She is scheduled to follow up with Dr. ___ in ___ 
___ clinic on ___.
.  
# Hyponatremia - Patient with Na 131 on discharge, versus normal 
at baseline.  TSH and cortisol were normal (in the absence of 
other signs of thyroid or adrenal dysfunction).  Given elevated 
urine osms and Na in the setting of hyponatremia, there may be a 
component of inappropriate ADH in this woman with recent 
vomiting.  We recommend follow up with her PCP in the coming 
weeks.
.  
# H/o GERD/esophagitis - The patient had a single guaiac + 
vomitus.  She was on IV followed by po PPI, which she will 
continue as an outpatient.
.
# Heart murmur / LV outflow tract obstruction: echo in ___ 
demonstrating mild LVH with resting LVOT gradient (30 mmHg) 
increased to 60 mmHg on valsalva, and aortic valve sclerosis.  
There was no evidence of endocarditis on this admission.  She 
was asked to follow up with her PCP regarding cardiology 
consultation and/or further imaging.
